pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards final score: Cade makes history in double OT win
pistons.body:
WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 12: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons celebrates against the Washington Wizards during the first overtime at Capital One Arena on November 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points, and the Detroit Pistons needed every single one of them in a 144-140 victory in double overtime against the Washington Wizards. It was not just a career-best night for Cunningham, not just one of the top-5 scoring performances in Pistons history, it was the first game in NBA history that saw a player score 50 points, dish 11 assists, and commit zero turnovers.

Cunningham simply did it all. He scored 30 points in the fourth quarter and overtime. That includes a critical 3-pointer after the Wizards had crawled their way back into the lead in the first overtime on an Anthony Davis alley-oop dunk.

The Pistons trailed 130-127 and each team had traded misses. Cunningham calmly took the ball up the left side of the floor, took a pass from Ausar Thompson, and walked into a movement 3-pointer that hit nothing but net to tie the game. On the next possession, Cade swung the ball to Duncan Robinson for what felt like a game-sealing 3 with 9 seconds left, but a video review determined Duncan had approximately 1 milimeter of his foot on the line and changed it to a two.

The scoring barrage also included critical stretch in the fourth quarter where he scored eight points and assisted another to account for 11 of Detroit’s final 12 points of the fourth quarter. Cunningham also locked up Trae Young on defense with Detroit up 119-118 in the final 30 seconds of the fourth. He forced Young into the sideline, cut off any passing lane, deflected the ball, and forced shot clock violation.

Sadly, after Cade hit two free throws to make it a 3-point game, Young redeemed himself by hitting an off-balance three from 29 feet away to give us our two overtimes of fun.

Cunningham’s performance slightly overshadowed another notable feat — Ausar Thompson tallied his first career triple-double. He was aggressive on offense driving to the rim, and delivered crisp passes in narrow lanes to keep Detroit’s offense moving.

On a night where Cade scores 52 and Ausar gets a triple-double, how the heck was it so close to begin with? How does a game like that feature 20 lead changes and 13 ties? It was a weird game.

Alex Sarr was 12-of-14 from the floor and hit his first four threes of the night. He scored 30 points and was one of three Wizards to hit the 30-point threshold. Young scored a team-high 37 points, including a perfect 17-of-17 from the line. Anthony Davis scored 30 points and added 15 rebounds.

Honestly, Detroit’s biggest issue was the same issue they’ve had all season. Their bigs were dominated and DEtroit really misses Jalen Duren. Washington outscored Detroit in the paint and were outrebounded. The biggest issue was John Collins yet again. He was a minus-18 on the night and it felt like it was even worse.

Collins started the overtime period at center in place of Paul Reed, who was a plus-25, and promptly was the primary factor in Detroit giving up a 7-0 run to the Wizards right out of the gate. It was ugly. Come back soon, Jalen Duren.

Yeah, the Pistons might be missing Duren something fierce, but they have Cade Cunningham. And that’s enough.

Rarely have I been so interested in an immediate rematch as I am in tonight’s game, which sees the Detroit Pistons taking on the Washington Wizards for the second consecutive contest. The Pistons prevailed in Monday’s game 122-111. The game was also just dang weird. Anthony Davis played out of his mind, scoring 44 points in just 34 minutes. Rookie AJ Dybantsa also enjoyed the best game of his young pro career, scoring 21 and securing eight rebounds. Everyone else on the Wizards was pretty stinky.

Conversely, Cade Cunningham had one of the worst games of the season, and Detroit was really propelled by some excellent play from John Collins and Daniss Jenkins in a new-look starting lineup. Gone are the mismatched pair of Paul Reed and Collins sharing the floor. In is Collins as a center with room to operate and Jenkins as a secondary ball handler. It’ll be interesting to see if they build off that success or if it was temporary. If Detroit can get both Collins and Jenkins playing at a high level and a locked-in Cade, it could be a blowout. If instead the Wizards bounce back, it could get messy.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Wizards preview:  Round two against the Wizards
pistons.body:
The Pistons and Wizards play each other again, but it is after 3 days of rest for the Pistons and the day after a game for the Wizards because the NBA used Chat GPT to generate the schedule this year or something.  This will only be the Pistons 3rd game in the last 8 days and their 2nd game against the Wizards.

The Pistons were able to control Monday’s game from start-to-finish, but the game was a little closer than it should have been because they had no answer for Anthony Davis.  Davis finished the game with 44 points and only missed 5 shots total.

The Pistons will still be without Jalen Duren, so they once again may struggle to guard Anthony Davis.  But, as Monday proved, even if they can’t stop Davis, they can still win if they stop the rest of the team.

Game Vitals

Where:  Capital One Arena in Washington DC
When:  Thursday, November 12 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  Scripps Sports Network
Odds:  Pistons (-10.5)

Analysis

There isn’t a ton more to say about this matchup that wasn’t very evident in Monday’s game.  With Jalen Duren out, the Pistons have no solution to opposing big men with any kind of offensive skill that are over 6’10”.  It seems hyperbolic, but it really has been the case.  Paul Reed is undersized and John Collins is not a natural center.  Tolu Smith has the size to possibly keep up, but he has proven to be out of his element pretty much any time he has gotten playing time so far.

The Pistons did opt to start John Collins at center against the Wizards on Monday and it did work out offensively, as he had a season-high 24 points.  But, the aforementioned Anthony Davis was able to cruise to 44 points without much resistance.  Anthony Davis always seems to have his best games against the Pistons and I wouldn’t expect him to hit a couple threes every single night, but a lot of the offense he was able to generate was off of offensive rebound putbacks or shots over the undersized players guarding him.

Surprisingly, the Pistons were only outrebounded 46-45, but they were outrebounded 14-11 on the offensive glass.  If you watched the game, you could see the Pistons lack of size rear it’s head countless times.  It is just the current state of things and something the Pistons will have to manage as best as they can for the next two weeks while Jalen Duren is still out with his hamstring injury.

The Pistons benefitted heavily from poor games out of Alex Sarr and Kyshawn George, which George in particular has been arguably the Wizards 2nd best player this season.  Trae Young also had a poor night from beyond the arc where he shot 3-of-10.  Some of that is because of how good the Pistons perimeter defense is and if the Pistons can replicate that tonight, it doesn’t really matter if they have nobody to slow down Anthony Davis.

AJ Dybantsa was able to get going a bit on Monday as he scored 21 points on 8-of-17 shooting.  There were times where he looked overwhelmed, as he had 5 turnovers, but he showed why he was the number 1 pick and a building block for the Wizards.  The Pistons have perimeter players to slow him down, but the refs were very whistle-happy on Monday which helped Dybantsa get momentum on his drives to the basket since the Pistons were not able to be as physical.

One small point of concern has been the play of Cade Cunningham over the last few games.  He had arguably his best game of the season a little over a week ago against the Charlotte Hornets and since then has really struggled, especially from beyond the arc.  He is 1 for his last 19 from beyond the arc after being close to 40% through the first seven games of the season.

He is playing more off-ball and getting clean looks, they just aren’t falling right now.  Teams are obviously focusing their defense more on Cade, but a lot of the current issues are just due to not being able to hit his outside shots.  Hopefully that changes tonight.

Luckily, Daniss Jenkins has been able to step up the last couple nights as he had a career-high, 31 points against the Lakers on Sunday and then 22 points, 6 rebounds, and 8 assists on Monday while starting.  Given the success the Pistons had starting him along with John Collins at center, I would suspect that they roll out that starting lineup again.

There were some issues defensively, which I already touched on, but the offense was much better with Collins starting and more-importantly, it finally got John Collins going after his early-season struggles.

If the Pistons are able to replicate the game they played on Monday, they shouldn’t have a difficult time defeating the Wizards, but if they let one of the other players besides Anthony Davis get hot, the Wizards have a shot at the upset.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (7-3):  Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

Washington Wizards (4-8):  Trae Young, Kyshawn George, AJ Dybantsa, Anthony Davis, Alex Sarr

Question of the Day

Do you think there is a solution to the Pistons big-man struggles or do they just need to ride it out until Jalen Duren returns?

DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 9: John Collins #20 of the Detroit Pistons dunks the ball in the game against the Washington Wizards on November 9, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. For those of you DBB sickos who care, I’m officially a married man! We had a spooky wedding on Halloween night and spent the past week in Cabo San Lucas for our honeymoon. We had a great time celebrating over the past week and a half!

Now we’re back to Pistons hoops.

JB Bickerstaff decided to mix up the starting lineup by starting John Collins at center. Paul Reed moved to the bench, and Daniss Jenkins was inserted into the starting lineup. Detroit started small with Duncan Robinson at the 3 and Ausar Thompson at the 4.

It proved to be the right idea early, as Collins was the leading scorer for Detroit after the first quarter with nine points. The Wizards took a 32-31 lead heading into the second, behind 12 points from Trae Young and 11 from Anthony Davis.

Detroit struggled to have an answer defensively for AD, and this was another game where Detroit missed Jalen Duren’s physicality and inside presence. Davis had 30 points and eight rebounds at the halfway point while only missing one of his 11 attempts. The Pistons put up 37 points in the quarter with five different players scoring more than seven points. Collins led the way with 15, Duncan had 14, and Cade had 11 as Detroit held a 68-58 lead.

The third quarter was all about Daniss Jenkins. Cade picked up his fifth foul halfway through the third, and DJ took the reins. He made Trae Young look like a traffic cone on defense as Jenkins went on to score 13 in the quarter. He consistently attacked Young, and Young never stood a chance. Detroit continued to extend their lead as they were up 103-87 heading into the fourth.

The fourth quarter was highlighted by two beautiful plays by Ebuka Okorie and Ausar Thompson.

First, watch Ausar find Okorie in transition as Okorie does his best Kyrie Irving impression:

AUSAR TO EBUKA WE ARE IN HEAVEN pic.twitter.com/jggv5WFEeC
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

Second, the Human Swiss Army knife blocks the 7-footer Alex Sarr on one end, then follows that up by directing traffic and finding an open DJ with a great bounce pass for a wide-open dunk:

Just let Ausar do everything pic.twitter.com/3nlVa0IHKi
— Rip Haminkton (@RedAlternates) November 10, 2026

The Pistons will continue to hope for a speedy recovery for Jalen Duren as they needed his inside physicality against Anthony Davis, who finished with 44 points and 13 rebounds while shooting 16-for-21 from the field. Detroit still managed to pull away with a 122-111 win behind three different players who scored 20+ points, despite none of them being Cade Cunningham.

John Collins, in his starting small-ball five role, led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, shooting 9-for-13 from the field. Both Daniss Jenkins and Duncan Robinson added 22 points each, and Jenkins led Detroit with eight assists. Your fun fact of the night: Robinson led the Pistons with seven free throw attempts. There has been a clear difference in his game this year as he looks to get to the line more often. Cunningham added 17 points and seven assists.

The Pistons improve to 7-3 on the season. Detroit’s home-and-home matchup with the Wizards continues as the Pistons will travel to Washington for Round 2 on Thursday night.

Go Stones.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 8: Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Detroit Pistons on November 8, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Brian Sevald/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren’t about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit’s point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

1. Kevin Huerter

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons’ rotation this season. In a game where Detroit’s entire backcourt didn’t really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he’d be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he’s hitting 40% from deep this season.

2. John Collins and Paul Reed

Detroit’s starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain’t pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it’s the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it’s two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It’s an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers’ big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion’s share of the blame goes to Collins. He’s been quite bad all season, and it’s getting less clear by the day how he’s going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don’t think he’s ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn’t surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

3. Austin Reaves

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he’d never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

4. Daniss Jenkins

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, “This is not going to happen.”

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He’s got scoring in his blood, and he’s more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard’s body. He’s got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he’s better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he’s not running the offense.

4. The refs.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

They arrived the day before the game and left as soon as it ended. Their opponents, the 49ers, spent an entire week in Australia before the season opener. The Rams got wiped by the 49ers, 27-7, leading many to believe travel plans were at fault for Los Angeles’ lackluster performance.

The difference between the Lions’ and Patriots’ approach to travel is obviously not as drastic. Twenty-four hours may not make that much of a difference, but there are bound to be some who believe the Lions didn’t take enough time to adjust. Lions coach Dan Campbell tried to assure media members in attendance in Munich that they will be more than ready for Sunday’s game.

“Very confident. Very confident. I know today will be the hardest day,” Campbell said.

The last 24 hours have undoubtedly been a grueling schedule for the players. Thursday in Detroit, they had a normal day of meetings, practice, and media availability. Hours later, they were on a flight to Munich, arriving around 8:30 a.m. local time (2:30 a.m. Detroit time). Using whatever energy they recaptured from sleeping on the plane, they went right into team meetings and a walkthrough practice.

“We went from the plane; we have got settled in. About an hour later we have got into meetings, and you’re doing a little bit of the head bob,” Campbell admitted.

Still, with over 48 hours to acclimate before kickoff, Campbell is certain the team will be more than ready for Sunday’s matchup with the Patriots.

“We have got up and moved around, and I know that every eight hours here, we’re going to begin to acclimate,” Campbell said. “I know by the time we hit Sunday morning into that Sunday afternoon game, we’re going to be ready to go. So, we will be primed and ready, and I feel very good about our plan.”

lions.headline: What it’s like to witness Dan Campbell win over a room of German reporters
lions.body:
Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell opened his Munich press conference—which was attended by nearly 100 media members—with an off-kilter story. When asked what German he’d learned from Amon-Ra St. Brown, he launched into a tale about wanting to spice up the term “spread your wings” with some good old-fashioned profanity. He wanted the f-word, and when he looked it up, the closest he got was “scheiße”—the word for shit. He went for it, essentially saying “spread your shit wings.”

For us who know Campbell, that kind of clunky story is part of his self-deprecating charm. It’s undeniably funny, but it didn’t really land with the German crowd. They were either unprepared for the untraditional cadence of Campbell, or something got lost in translation.

However, for the next 20 minutes, I was able to witness what is truly a joy every time I get the opportunity to do so: watching Dan Campbell win over a room. As the mostly German press got a crash course on Campbell’s folksy accent and imperfect diction, they were also treated to his charm and authenticity. My attention quickly turned from Campbell’s answers to the media members consuming his words.

The cracked smiles that eventually gave way to unstoppable laughter. The nods of shared experience. The realization by some that they better get their phones out before this incredible answer ended.

There were two answers in Friday’s press conference where Campbell shined the most and left the crowded pub-turned-media room beaming. The first was when Campbell was asked about making his pitch for an international fan to become a Lions fan. Campbell, instead, made an entire argument for the game of football.

Campbell, as he often does when he’s about to drop bars, took his time to really think it through before answering.

“I was fortunate enough to be able to play this game before I coached it. I got to play 11 seasons. I think this is my 28th year in the NFL. I think it’s 28,” Campbell said, as he ramped up the passion. “This game, this game gave me a life, okay? I was not a superstar. I was not a speed demon. I’ve got size. I played tight end, so you do a little bit of everything. But it gave me an opportunity to make a life and do something I absolutely loved with a group of guys—at any given time, 53 men that have the same goal, and you’re all going in the same direction, and the blood and the sweat and the tears that it requires on a daily basis to be great are things you never forget.”

Buckle up, he’s just getting started.

“And it builds character. It builds character in your team, it builds character in your individual, and it allows you overcome anything in life that may come your way. I tell the team all the time, one day you’re going to get hit; you’re going to get rocked with something really tough in your life. And I hate to say it, I don’t want it to happen, none of us do, but you will. And you’re going to have to be the rock, but you’re going to know how to overcome it, and you know who you can lean on, too: your brothers who have gone through everything you’ve had to go through here.”

Campbell then snapped out of his own trance, as he often does after a long, passionate answer.

“I just think it’s special that way. And it gives guys an opportunity that may not have all the bells and whistles—just because they do all the little things right and they maximize everything that they have in their ability.”

Now drive it home with some humbleness.

“That’s the best way I could do it or say it.”

The NFL may as well cut that answer together right now, and play it at every event in which they’re trying to grow the game. But Campbell wasn’t done.

Then he cut a promo specifically about the city of Detroit and how it has shaped his football team.

“We don’t have the beach. We don’t have all this—now the summers are unbelievable, but things come a little bit harder out in that area,” Campbell said. “I always equate it to: it’s people that’ll do anything for you. They’d give you the shirt off their back if you needed it. And they’re all about doing the hard stuff.

“And when I came to Detroit to take over as head coach, man, I wanted to build a team that they could relate to. We want to be a team that they can look at and say, ‘I respect that. I respect the way they go about their business.’ That there is something gritty about it. It is hard work. It is inspiring football. It’s not the easy way out.’

“And so those are really the type of fans we have, man. Just good, wholesome people that really care about each other. They put in good days’ work and man, they back us up and support the heck out of us, and we love them to death.”

Throw some dramatic music behind that, play it before kickoff at Ford Field, and welcome the thousands of German fans who are now ready to ride with Detroit.

Campbell’s German may not go beyond “guten tag” and “scheiße,” but there is something he shares in common with the country’s culture. And he was sure to mention it in his perfect press conference dismount.

“You don’t come to Germany without getting a German beer. I know that. So, I will definitely have a beer before I leave, that’s for sure. I don’t know which one or what, but I’m getting one.”

After the dust has settled, a German reporter gleefully turned to the local Detroit beat writers and asked a question we’re accustomed to answering in the States.

“Is he always like that?”

Yes. Yes, he is.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Patriots: 3 key matchups for Week 10
lions.body:
Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff is hit by Miami Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson (44) during the first half at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Right tackle Blake Miller blocks. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

It’s Germany week as the Detroit Lions (6-2) travel abroad to take on the New England Patriots (5-4). Buckle up. It is about to be a wild 11-day gauntlet as the Lions play the Patriots, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Chicago Bears in that span.

Meanwhile, the NFC North is absolutely insane. I love it.

This is how it was always meant to be. This is adversity.

Turn on local Detroit radio, and you’ll likely hear voices of doubt and concern. Switch to national outlets, and you’ll hear the Bears declared the favorites in the NFC, Jordan Love MVP discourse, and Kirk Cousins transforming the Vikings’ outlook as contenders.

I love it. This is how it was always meant to be.

With a win on Sunday, the Lions will take over the top spot in the NFC North with the Chicago Bears on their bye. In that event, the Lions will be 7-2 and 2-0 in the division, whereas the Bears will also be 7-2, but 0-2 in the division. All signs point to an absolute battle on Thanksgiving, as Ford Field will undoubtedly, again, welcome Ben Johnson with echoing boos.

But first, taking care of business against the Patriots and Buccaneers is priority one.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities to control the division.

Blake Miller vs. Gabe Jacas

The first key matchup is rookie versus rookie. New England’s second-round pick, EDGE rusher Gabe Jacas, Illinois, has been a disruptive playmaker from the start. For Grit Index followers, his name is not new. Jacas was one of the guys we were pounding the table for here, leading all EDGE rushers with a 9.14 Grit Index score. The Lions went with Derrick Moore, to my surprise. But an uncertain knee injury for Jacas became known after the draft process that may have been one of the contributing factors for the Lions to favor Moore.

Jacas’ early play has been impressive both as a pass rusher as well as a run defender.

#Patriots rookie EDGE Gabe Jacas continues to flash on tape. His sudden movements to shed run blocks like he does in the first clip with a swim move are impressive.

Also showed good burst to close the pocket as a looper on a stunt for a sack. pic.twitter.com/kagHHFv8fg
— Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) November 2, 2026

He plays violently with a relentless motor.

The Gabe Jacas film is so good, guys. #Patriots rookie winning with power, quickness, bend around the arc and play recognition. High level stuff. pic.twitter.com/s9i2ZJab3d
— Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) October 23, 2026

On the other side, however, the Lions have had a strong start from right tackle Blake Miller, who has had more ups than downs in his rookie campaign. Last week, however, was notably more down than his average performance.

Blake Miller is having a hard time with the Dolphins edge speed on pass rushes
— Erik Schlitt (@erikschlitt) November 8, 2026

When Jacas is lines up over Miller, my eyes will be on how the Lions’ rookie tackle responds. It will be an entertaining matchup, for sure, but also the winner of it will have a say in which team has a better flight back across the Atlantic.

Christian Mahogany vs. Christian Mahogany

The next matchup is all between the ears for left guard Christian Mahogany. After a benching for breaking team rules last week, Mahogany is back in the starting lineup. It became apparent watching the game against the Miami Dolphins that the Lions’ best five along the offensive line includes Mahogany, as Miles Frazier’s struggles impacted the Lions’ typically potent offense.

“Look, if you say you’re gonna do something, you better hold up to it, otherwise you’re gonna lose respect of the people around you,” said Dan Campbell on 97.1 The Ticket. “Because if I’m sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don’t do it, I would immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we’re gonna do here.”

It is time for Mahogany to take the next step as a professional. He knows it.

Lions guard Christian Mahogany did not shed light on what team rules he broke, but talked about being benched last Sunday.

"I have to grow up," he said. "I let my teammates down, I let my organization down, and it won't ever happen again." pic.twitter.com/hx7ZhCRkMZ
— Brad Galli (@BradGalli) November 11, 2026

The time is now. If not now, Dan Campbell surely will not let one player hold the rest of the team back.

Patriots’ rookie cornerbacks vs. Lions receiving corps

With veteran cornerback Carlton Davis III already ruled out for the game, the Patriots will be leaning on two rookies to play the role opposite Christian Gonzalez. The two rookies are fifth-round pick Karon Prunty, Wake Forest, and undrafted free agent Channing Canada, TCU.

Following up on an abysmal performance against the Green Bay Packers’ paper tiger deep passing attack, the New England secondary will face an even more difficult matchup against the Lions. Following Jared Goff’s first game of the season without a passing touchdown and back-to-back games with an interception, ending his early-season streaks, Goff will be looking to right the ship against the Patriots. If I were a betting man, an Amon-Ra St. Brown anytime touchdown in his home country of Germany may be the safest bet of the weekend.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities.

lions.headline: What are your plans for the Lions game in Germany?
lions.body:
If you haven’t heard yet, the Detroit Lions are playing a game in Munich, Germany, this weekend. The team made the trip across the pond Thursday after practice, but many members of the media and the fanbase have already been in town for a few days, soaking up everything Munich and the surrounding areas have to offer. From scenic pictures of the nature outside the city, to the architecture, music, and food within, it looks like Lions fans are having a great time on their Fall vacations. This week has been fun following along with fans who made the trip.

However, for those of us who didn’t catch a flight to Germany, we are preparing for a whole new game day experience. And if you look at the schedule, this is technically a home game for Detroit, which dramatically changes things for those of us who attend the home games at Ford Field. For those who live outside of Southeast Michigan, it may not feel all that different, apart from the 9:30 am kickoff. Maybe you live on the West Coast, and you may have to set an alarm to ensure you are up for the start of the game.

That brings us to today’s question of the day:

What are your plans for the Lions’ international game against the New England Patriots?

My answer: I plan to make a big breakfast early in the morning for my family and a few friends to eat around 8:30 am, then lock in for kickoff as if it were an away game. Saturday morning we will head over to Gratiot Central Market, grab our necessary items for the breakfast feast, and hopefully get to bed early Saturday night so that smoker is fired up and ready to roll by 7:30 am Sunday morning. My only question is whether I will transition from coffee to a few Miller High Lifes before kickoff or not.

What about you? What are your plans for the Lions’ Week 10 game in Germany? Let us know in the comments below.

lions.headline: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Patriots in Week 10
lions.body:
Nov 12, 2026; Munich, Germany; The jerseys of Detroit Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (97) and wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) and New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) at the Galeria Munchen Marienplatz. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Lions (6-2) and New England Patriots (5-4) will face off in a Week 10 interconference battle in Munich, Germany.

“We understand the challenge here,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Patriots. “It’s a very good team. It’s a competitive team. They’re going to clean up a lot of things, and we’ve got to be ready to go.”

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 2.5-point favorites in Week 10. Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Patriots in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

Patriots base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 10 preview: Breaking down the Patriots’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Gibbs attacks the EDGE in the run game

The Lions and Patriots both have old-school coaches who are both direct or indirect descendants of the Bill Parcells coaching tree. And as you might expect, like Parcells, both coaches prioritize controlling the trenches by establishing the run on offense and stopping the run on defense.

By the numbers, the Patriots’ run defense looks strong. They’re 10th in DVOA run defense, ninth in rush yards allowed per game (96.7) and per play (3.9), fifth in EPA per rush (-0.12), and third in yards before contact (0.57). Their success ties to a strong interior defensive line that can stuff the run in two- and three-down sets, featuring Milton Williams, Christian Barramore, and former Lion Corey Durden. It’s tough to find room up the gut.

Complicating things even further is how the Patriots deploy the blitz. Entering this game, the Patriots blitz 40.1% of the time (6th most in the NFL), and most of those blitzes come from their linebackers and come straight down the pipe—stressing the A and B gaps.

However, teams run outside on Patriots 53.8% of the time (10th highest rate) because their EDGE players are more skilled as pass rushers and can be overwhelmed in the run game. Their vulnerability shows up most in explosive plays. Currently, the Patriots allow an explosive run on 10.9% of rushing attempts (20th), have allowed 22 rushes over 10 yards this season, and average 3.31 yards allowed after contact (24th).

When we flip to the Lions’ rushing attack, we can see how they match up with the Patriots’ weaknesses. The Lions run the ball on the edges 55.7% of the time (7th), lead the NFL in explosive run plays (16.5% of the time), have 33 rushes of 10+ yards (3rd), and average 3.15 yards after contact (10th).

If the Patriots blitz and the Lions attack the edge, Jahmyr Gibbs will have a chance to eat.

Prediction 2: Goff finds success with quick hitters and deep shots

The Patriots’ defensive line is built to stop the run up the middle, create pressure off the edge and with blitzing linebackers, then deploy their secondary in nickel sets 77.7% of the time (2nd most in the NFL) and run man coverage out of it 36% of the time (2nd).

While chunk yards on the ground will certainly soften the Patriots’ defense, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will likely be the key to winning this game because he matches up so well with their coverage scheme. This season, Goff has an EPA of 40.57 vs. nickel defenses (2nd highest in the NFL), a per-play EPA of 0.23 vs. nickel (4th), and a per-play EPA of 0.36 vs. man coverage (3rd).

What makes it worse for the Patriots is that their coverage has been exposed in recent weeks, especially by NFC North teams. Last week against the Packers, the Patriots surrendered 372 passing yards to Jordan Love, and 308 to Bears QB Caleb Williams two weeks prior. Those struggles have shown up in their EPA numbers, too. On the season, the Patriots allow a per-pass play EPA of 0.07 (26th), but over the past four weeks, that number has plummeted to 0.35 (31st)

Goff’s key will be efficiency with short routes and a willingness to test them deep. When the Patriots are in off coverage, use the space against them. When they blitz, having quick-hitter answers in the vacated space behind them will lead to yards after catch (YAC). Then, when success comes underneath with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta, test them with deep shots to Jameson Williams.

Prediction 3: Lions focus on stopping the run; contain Maye

As mentioned earlier, the Patriots want to control the game on the ground, but their results haven’t matched their dedication. The Patriots run the ball on 46% of offensive plays (10th most) and gain 119.9 yards per game (10th), but their per-play efficiency is more middle-of-the-road.

As a team, they average 4.2 yards per rush (14th), but only Drake Maye and RB3 Corey Kiner average above 4.0 yards per carry; RB1 Rhamondre Stevenson and RB2 TreVeyon Henderson average 3.9 yards per carry. We see similar results in EPA and success rate. The team’s EPA per run is -0.02 (11th), while Stevenson (-0.06) and Henderson (-0.28) fall below the average. The team’s rushing success rate is 41.8% (14th), while Stevenson is close at 40.2, but Henderson is well below at 34.6%.

The high volume of run plays can make a middle-of-the-road rushing attack look better than it is, but the real catalyst skewing the numbers is quarterback Drake Maye’s mobility. Maye has carried the ball 47 times through nine games, averages 4.7 yards per carry, has a per-play rushing EPA of +0.40, and a 51.1% success rate.

Aside from a poor first quarter against Bills QB Josh Allen in Week 2 (when he gained 40 of his 69 rushing yards that day), the Lions defense has done a good job handling mobile quarterbacks this season. Vikings Kyler Murray gained 35 yards in Week 8, but no other quarterback has rushed for 20 yards against the Lions defense: Jacoby Brissett had 19 yards, Geno Smith (12), Tyler Shough (8), Malik Willis (7, groin injury), and Bryce Young (3) were all held under 20 rushing yards.

Defenses have deployed a spy on Maye situationally, and I expect the Lions to do the same in this game.

Prediction 4: McNeill pressures the middle of the OL

The Patriots offensive line has dealt with several injuries this season, and they’ve struggled to keep pressure at bay. Entering this game, they’ve allowed 141 pressures (28th) and a 42.9% pressure rate (31st). Maye has done a nice job handling the extra pressure for the most part, only taking 20 sacks (17th) with a 6.6% sack rate (18th), but it has led to him making some poor choices with the football; he is currently tied for the most interceptions in the NFL with 11.

So where are the weaknesses in the line? Right up the middle.

New England lost both starting guards—Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu—to injured reserve. Backup Greg Van Roten was injured in the one game he started, landed on injured reserve, and has only recently opened his injury evaluation window. Backup center Ben Brown was then called up to shift to guard, but he’s been dealing with an injury and has been ruled out for this game. Finally, Walter Rouse has been supplementing/rotating with Brown at left guard, but he is currently in concussion protocol.

Heading into this game, Matt Pryor has started at right guard the last three games and is expected to maintain that role, but left guard is still up in the air. The Patriots likely need Rouse to clear concussion protocol or Van Roten to be activated from injured reserve and step into a starting role.

Regardless of where they land at left guard, they’ll have the unenviable task of trying to block Alim McNeill.

Pass rush win rate vs. pressure rate for pass rushing defensive tackles pic.twitter.com/lQDKjlIsi0
— Ray Carpenter (@csv_enjoyer) November 10, 2026

McNeill has been a monster this season, as teams have had to deal with the totality of the Lions defensive line. Most teams have focused heavily on Aidan Hutchinson, but the developmental progression of Tyleik Williams, a wonderful rookie season for Skyler Gill-Howard, the steady veteran presence of DJ Wonnum, and the recent emergence of rookie Derrick Moore have allowed McNeill to flourish even more.

Through eight games, according to the Lions PR, McNeill is:

1st in games with 0.5 sacks (6)

1st in QB hurries (24)

2nd in total pressures generated (34)

2nd in sacks (5.5)

t-4th in QB hits (10)

McNeill taking advantage of the reserve guards could be a huge factor in this game. If the Lions rush four and drop seven, and the Patriots need to keep players in for Hutchinson and McNeill, Maye will have fewer targets and a muddied back-seven to sort through.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions vs. New England Patriots preview, prediction: On Paper
lions.body:
Nov 12, 2026; Munich, Germany; Detroit Lions hats with 2026 NFL Munich Game patch at the NFL Shop Munich. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Lions and New England Patriots are in Germany for a big international matchup. The Patriots are a bit desperate for a win, sitting at 5-4 and clinging to the final playoff spot in the AFC. The Lions are a little more comfortable in the fifth spot of the NFC playoff race, but if they want to contend in a competitive NFC North, they need this game, too.

So which team has that statistical advantage and will come out on top Sunday morning? Let’s dive into the numbers with our Week 10 Lions vs. Patriots On Paper preview and prediction.

Note: Stats may be a little lighter this week because one of my bigger resources—NFL Pro—is not available in Germany.

Lions pass offense (12th in DVOA) vs. Patriots pass defense (15th)

The Detroit Lions had their worst passing offense performance last week against a bad—but improving—Dolphins defense. Offensive line struggles were the lowlight of the performance, headlined by the “suspension” of left guard Christian Mahogany and inconsistent play of rookie right tackle Blake Miller. Mahogany is back in the lineup, and that should help the Lions’ passing offense which has remained near a top-five unit for most of the season. They rank:

Fourth in passer rating (106.5)

Seventh in yards per attempt (7.8)

Fourth in dropback EPA (0.237)

Fourth in dropback success rate (51.0%)

And despite the poor offensive performance, the Lions offensive line is still grading out well as a unit. Though they rank 17th in sack percentage (6.5), they’re fifth in pressure percentage allowed (19.4%), second in PFF pass blocking grade (75.1), and seventh in pass block win rate (54%).

The Patriots pass defense started off strong, but has struggled as of late, even against some of the most medicore-to-bad passing offenses. For the season, they rank:

27th in passer rating (100.2)

25th in yards per attempt (7.9)

24th in dropback EPA (0.151)

25th in dropback success rate (48.4%)

For comparison’s sake, all of these rankings except for dropback EPA are below the Lions’ pass defense. So whatever you think of Detroit’s ability to defend the pass, the Patriots have been worse.

But much like Detroit’s pass defense, the one place they thrive is pressuring the opposing quarterback. Thought they’re just 19th in pressure percentage (22.4), they’re sixth in sack rate (8.0%), 11th in pass rush win rate (52%), and second in PFF pass rush grade (82.8).

While EDGE Elijah Ponder leads the team with 7.5 sacks, it’s really New England’s interior pressure that causes havoc. Look out for Christian Barmore (78.1 PFF pass rush grade) and Milton Williams (20 pressures) to give Detroit’s interior offensive line some issues.

But New England’s second is very beatable. Christian Gonzalez is having a down year (50.4 PFF grade) and the Patriots will be down Carlton Davis.

Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. This isn’t just a Germany thing, St. Brown should thrive against the Patriots’ zone-heavy defense. Brown is the Lions’ best weapon when it comes to recognizing the soft spot in zones, just like last week’s eight-catch, 86-yard performance.

Advantage: Lions +2.5. The Patriots’ pass rush does have a chance to disrupt Jared Goff like the Dolphins did last week, but for most of the day, the Lions quarterback should be picking apart this poor secondary.

Lions run offense (4th) vs. Patriots run defense (10th)

The inconsistency of this rushing attack is still very frustrating to watch, but putting things into perspective, it’s still a very decent run game in Detroit. For the season, they rank:

10th in yards per carry (4.4)

12th in rush EPA (-0.073)

Third in rush success rate (46.0%(

Negative plays remain a huge problem, with Detroit’s 20% stuffed rate ranking 25th in the NFL. They are improving in short-yardage situations, though, climbing to 18th in power success rate.

Still, the offensive line—though still plagued by some mental mistakes—appear to be moving people. Detroit ranks fourth in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and, as a whole, the Lions entire team is fourth in PFF’s run blocking grade.

Detroit will face a formidable test this week against a run defense that has allowed 100 rushing yards just three times this entire season, and each of their last five opponents have been held at or below 4.0 yards per carry. Though last week’s performance against the Packers’ worst rushing attack in the league should provide at least some hope.

For the season, the Patriots rank:

Ninth in yards per carry allowed (3.9)

10th in rush EPA (-0.123)

11th in rush success rate (36.9%)

Interestingly, the Patriots run defense appears more efficient than the sum of their parts. They rank just 16th in adjusted line yards allowed, 16th in run stop win rate, and 21st in PFF run defense grade.

One thing they do thrive in, however, is limiting explosives. They’ve only allowed six rushing plays of 15+ yards (third fewest) and just a single run of 20+ yards (t-fewest). But they’re just okay in short-yardage situations. They’re 10th in power success rate allowed (59%), but sport just a 16% stuffed rate (23rd).

Player to watch: LB Christian Ellis. While the Patriots are not particularly strong up the middle in run defense, Ellis sports the eighth-best PFF grade against the run (82.3), providing a strong second level of defense. The Patriots’ secondary is also active and strong against the run.

Advantage: Lions +0.5. Detroit hasn’t been as explosive as expected running the football this year, but they have found some consistency running for gains of 5-10 yards, and that could be exactly what we see on Sunday.

Patriots pass offense (6th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th)

Despite a horrible start to the year, Drake Maye has seemingly righted the ship—outside of last week’s performance against a very solid Packers pass defense. For the entire year, the Patriots pass offense ranks:

11th in passer rating (96.2)

Third in yards per attempt (8.4)

10th in dropback EPA (0.162)

Third in dropback success rate (51.0%)

Essentially, if the Patriots could stop turning the ball over, they’d be a top-five passing attack. But turnovers have been a serious problem. Maye’s 11 interceptions leads the league and his 4.0% interception percentage is third-highest in the NFL. To sport that dishonor and still produce the 10th-highest dropback EPA is pretty crazy.

So what’s causing the high interception rate? It’s a little bit of everything. An injured offensive line that ranks 21st in pressure rate (23.6%) and 18th in sack rate (6.6%), a quarterback who is still young and figuring things out, and a receiving corps that lost Romeo Doubs for the season and hasn’t had a lot of A.J. Brown available.

But, again, the Patriots passing attack remains pretty dang efficient despite those problems.

I’m still hesitant to believe in Detroit’s defensive improvement through the air. Much of that appears based on simply playing a bunch of poor passing attacks, but the one aspect they have seriously improved on is explosive plays allowed. In the first four games, the Lions allowed 20 passing plays of 20 yards (most in NFL). In the last four games, the Lions have allowed 14 (still t-10th most). For the season, Detroit still only ranks:

24th in passer rating allowed (97.5)

18th in yards per attempt (7.2)

26th in dropback EPA (0.177)

24th in dropback success rate (48.3%)

The pass rush (eighth in sack rate, seventh in pressure rate) remains solid, despite an ever-decreasing blitz rate (26.3%, 18th).

Detroit will be without top cornerback D.J. Reed for at least another week, but Brian Branch’s return has allowed them to have a little more flexibility in their coverages, and it has calmed some things down (a little).

Player to watch: Hunter Henry. While Henry is far from 100% as he deals with a foot injury, he remains the biggest threat to Detroit’s defense. Henry is first on the team in receptions (32) and second in yards (361). Meanwhile, the Lions is 31st in DVOA vs. tight ends.

Advantage: Patriots +3. This is the matchup that could change the game. New England, in my opinion, have one of the best passing attacks as long as they can avoid turnovers. The Lions aren’t particularly great at forcing turnovers, creating just eight on the season—only three teams have fewer. So I would expect a pretty strong day from Maye.

Patriots run offense (19th) vs. Lions run defense (22nd)

New England hasn’t run the ball very consistently, although injuries have played a large part in that, particularly as of late. They have a fullback, a running back, and three offensive linemen on IR. Running back TreVeyon Henderson has already been ruled out this week and top running back Rhamondre Stevenson could miss this one, too. Guard Ben Brown has been declared out already, and his backup Walter Rouse is working his way through concussion protocol. Put it all together, and the Patriots’ running game ranks:

14th in yards per carry (4.2)

24th in rush EPA (-0.149)

21st in rushing success rate (36.8%)

That said, running back Corey Kiner has stepped in and provided a bit of a spark in the last two weeks, rushing for 93 yards on just 15 carries, bolstered by a couple of 20-yard runs. Additionally, they are great in short-yardage situations, converting 75% of power situations, ranking fifth in the NFL.

The Lions’ run defense is really starting to come on in recent weeks, with one of their best performances coming last week against a sneaky-good Dolphins run game. Overall, though, the numbers remain pretty pedestrian. The Lions rank:

18th in yards per carry allowed (4.1)

13th in rush EPA (-0.115)

Eighth in rush success rate (35.7%)

They’re still being victimized by some early-season explosives given up, but that has settled down considerably as of late.

What has been true pretty much all season is that Detroit has clogged the middle of the field. Led by the strong play of defensive tackles Tyleik Williams and Alim McNeill, anything between the b-gaps has been out of business. Yet, oddly, the Lions rank dead last in power success rate allowed, ceding an 84% conversion rate. So don’t expect many third-and-1 stops from Detroit on Sunday.

Player to watch: Malcolm Rodriguez. Rodriguez is quietly having a very strong season, and with Jack Campbell out for the foreseeable future, his role will continue to increase. Currently, he sports an 83.9 PFF run defense grade (seventh in NFL among LBs) and the third-highest run stop percentage (11.7).

Advantage: Lions +1. With all of the injuries, I just can’t trust the Patriots’ rushing attack. And given that the Lions finally seem to have some answers on defense, this should favor the Lions. The one aspect that could tilt things in New England’s favor, though, is Maye. While he still prefers to throw when he has escaped the pocket, he still does have 219 rushing yards this season, fourth most among quarterbacks.

Last week’s prediction:

While On Paper got wins both straight up and against the spread (6-2 overall, 4-4 ATS), it may have been my least accurate column of the year. I overestimated the Lions’ advantage on offense and underestimated their advantages on defense. I expected a shootout and got a 19-9 win, instead. Sure, I had no idea Mahogany was going to be out, but that doesn’t justify how bad I missed on that one.

To be fair, no one really expected a defensive battle. And the closest prediction in the comment section wasn’t all that close: a 24-16 prediction from The Proudest:

I don’t have photoshop on the road with me in Germany, so as your prize, enjoy this picture of me with a humongous beer in Munich:

This week’s prediction:

The Lions come out with a slight +1 advantage, but the edge in three of the four matchups. As is the case with a lot of games this year, the outcome could come down to that one disadvantage: the Lions’ pass defense. Maye is an electric player with a ton of explosive play potential. Detroit has done better at limiting that as of late, but the only recent quarterback they’ve played who can consistently do that was Jordan Love. If Detroit can repeat their performance from that game, they’ll be in good shape. If not, it could be a long flight home.

Lions 31, Patriots 30.

lions.headline: Before the Roar: Previewing Detroit Lions vs. New England Patriots
lions.body:
After a gritty, grind-it-out win in Week 9 over the Miami Dolphins, the 6-2 Detroit Lions are set to cross the Atlantic for a Week 10 clash with the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. As part of the NFL’s continuing efforts to grow the league’s popularity on a global scale, this trip for Detroit feels as though it has been in the works for a while—especially given the roots of All-Pro receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown. To preview the inter-conference matchup, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with the newest iteration of “Before the Roar.”

For starters, we dive into the play of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye. Simply put, Maye is an ascending player with all the athletic upside a team could want in a modern-day NFL quarterback. At the same time, New England’s offense has been a boom-or-bust unit for most of the season, and Maye is at the center of many of those turnover struggles. From there, we discuss how New England will adjust to losing their top two running backs and what the Lions’ defense can do to make Maye’s trip to Germany one he’ll soon want to forget.

On the defensive side of the ball, we highlight New England’s stout run defense and how Detroit can counter their aggressive front seven. We also highlight some of the struggles the Patriots have been dealing with in their secondary. Cornerback Carlton Davis III has already been ruled out, and Christian Gonzalez has struggled since returning from injury earlier this year.

To catch the whole episode, you can watch here, as well as listen wherever you get your podcasts.

If you haven’t already done so, please be sure to like and subscribe to the Pride of Detroit YouTube channel so you can stay up to date on all of the content we are putting out, including our annual charity drive taking place in November.

The Lions continue to get Joseph as much work as possible; even though he’s ruled out of this Sunday’s game, he got in a full practice on Thursday. Joseph is nearing the end of his injury evaluation window, and a decision on the future of his season will come early next week.

St. Brown is nursing a rib injury, but all indications are that he’ll be a go on Sunday. On any given week, it’s challenging to slow him down so his body can recover, but with the importance of this game to him and his family, he’s surely doing everything he can to be ready.

Michigan Wolverines head coach Kyle Whittingham smiles as he observes warmups ahead of a game against UTEP at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor on Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Michigan Wolverines are 5-4, and it’s been an underwhelming first season for head coach Kyle Whittingham. Could Whittingham be one-and-done? Most fans think so.

Earlier this week, we asked fans if they believe Michigan should fire Whittingham — and the results are telling.

michigan.headline: Preview: Oregon 2026
michigan.body:
Preview: Oregon 2026

Brian
November 13th, 2026 at 4:51 PM

Essentials
WHAT
Michigan (5-4, 2-4 Big Ten) vs
#18 Oregon (6-3, 4-2 Big Ten)

WHERE
Autzen Stadium
Eugene, OR

WHEN
3:30 Saturday
THE LINE
M +10.5 (Vegas)
M +9.5 (SP+)
TELEVISION
FS1
PBP: Tim Brando
Color: Devin Gardner
TICKETS
From $87
WEATHER
Cloudy, around 60, minimal chance of rain
Overview
We are at the juncture. We have been at the juncture before. We are here again. There is a football game in front of us. It will be played; some of us will watch it. We will care about it in the way we still can. In my case this will be staring dead eyed at the television until Michigan is down significantly, and then it will be splitting my attention between the game and garbage people post on the internet.
Whatever you do from here on out is between you and God. Ain't no one judging you. Unless you do crimes. Do not do crimes.
[AFTER THE JUMP: gallows humor]

Run Offense vs Oregon

no [Barron]
I have at times wanted to make a section of this preview just this:
No.

Every previous time I have wanted to do this it is because Michigan's defense was so overwhelming and the opposition offense so anemic that the prospect of the opponent doing something meaningful was barely worth addressing. Now the tables have turned.
Late against Michigan State, Michigan brought in Babalola and Walbridge at tackle. Evan Link moved inside to guard and Frazier exited. Frazier is listed as doubtful on the injury report; I would be surprised if he continues sticking it out through an injury when the sensible thing to do now is to recover and prepare for 2027. I imagine Nathan Efobi is still healthy so if I had to guess I'd bet the line this week is Link/Efobi/Guarnera/Norton/Babalola, for what little that matters.
Dumping Jason Beck was necessary—rumor has it that Michigan might not have had an offense to put on the plane if they had not—but Michigan's issues are so baked-in at this point, and the personnel so suddenly substandard everywhere except wide receiver, that I expect little if any dead cat bounce in this game. A shuffled OL, a banged-up running back room, an incoherent offense no one understands: these issues are still there even if Jim Harding will be calling base run plays Michigan has not been able to run at all this year.
For what it's worth, Oregon's rush defense has been completely unpredictable week to week. They were gashed by Oklahoma State (237 yards, 5.9 a pop), Illinois (225/5.7) and Northwestern (175/4.9) but suffocated Boise State and Nebraska. Games against OSU, UCLA, and USC are somewhere in the middle. Fun fact: Oregon's worst run D PFF grade of the year is a 57 against OSU, when the Buckeyes ran for 76 yards on 19 carries.
Not that it will matter.
KEY MATCHUP: No.
Pass Offense vs Oregon

Obi Wan, you're my only hope [Paul Sherman]
As is the case with many young quarterbacks, Tommy Carr's initial flash of promise has given way to a lot of indecision and confusion. Carr added six relatively easy inaccurate passes last week. Carr has some mobility and may be able to get there but the current combination of freshman indecision and normie arm strength has made the sledding tough. Adding a bunch of flat-out misses made it untenable against MSU. At the same time Michigan's previous impregnable pass protection evaporated. After starting the season 1st in PFF pass block grading, they fell to 15th after MSU.
So this is pretty much also "no."
The thing Michigan has going for them is they have two dudes at WR and star corner Ify Obidegwu can only cover one of them. The second corner, Na'eem Offord, nearly got a cyan from Alex:
He's weaker than his peers and an egregiously poor tackler. I would look at whichever receiver is matched up on Offord and throw that direction.

Offord is 6'1" and is a former five star so there's probably something in there; if Oregon sticks Offord on Buchanan he may have the ability to stick with him and contest. Four PBUs on 35 targets is a pretty good rate even if it's nowhere near Obidegwu; I would not expect Offord to get wrecked as Buchanan sprints to a 200-yard day. He may give up a couple chunks.
And that's assuming a pass even gets off. After a season of mediocre opposition DEs Michigan steps it up this weekend. While Teitum Tuoti and his 18% win rate are out for the season, Oregon will try to make do with… two other guys with 18% win rates. Star Matayo Uiagalelei will be a menace liable to overwhelm anyone who gets chucked out there and rotational end Nasir Wyatt is an Uche/Stewart 6'1" missile. Since Wyatt is that and Oregon also has a big ol' anchor type in Elijah Rushing who will also see more playing time it may behoove Michigan to throw on standard downs if Rushing is out there. On the other hand, putting the burly run defender guy on the field seems like an entirely unnecessary adaptation to the Michigan rush offense.
Unless Andrew Babalola is an instant first rounder, the presumed absence of Frazier should put Michigan in MAC "not in the face" mode; I expect some fades and a bunch of short stuff that doesn't work nearly as much as it needs to.
KEY MATCHUP: MARSH AND BUCHANAN vs MOSSING MICHIGAN TO A WIN. If these guys go 12/12 on contested opportunities Michigan can win.
Run Defense vs Oregon

Seth on the season preview podcast
We did a preview podcast, as we do every year. We say many things. Some of them are right (everything we said about the defense) and some are wrong (everything we said about the offense except Marsh and Buchanan). Few takes are as out of left field and correct as Seth's seemingly random slander of the Oregon offensive line in our conference preview. I was skeptical, but here is rush EPA/play this year:

Your first thought there is probably "I had no idea Michigan was that high." Granted. The second most boggling thing about the above is that meep-meep Oregon is 11 freakin' spots worse than Michigan. That ranking is reflected in Oregon's PFF score. We take their run block grading somewhat lightly but they are 98th, more or less in line with their statistical output.
(I wonder if there's any value in comparing EPA/rush to PFF grade. Sometimes you have situations where the blocking is about the results (Oregon), situations where the blocking is better than the results (Michigan, which is 69th in run block grade), and the utterly inexplicable (Northwestern, 18th in EPA/rush and 95th in run block grade).
Anyway, this is a bad offensive line that got worse after injuries to both starting guards; a non-injury midseason switch at tackle also speaks to instability in the unit. Alex cyaned the right side of the line and didn't seem to  be too far away from issuing one on the left. Meanwhile half of the planned RB platoon is out; Jordon Davison hurt his leg against OSU. Dierre Hill is the primary option, and since he's been clearly the better back this year—50% more missed tackles forced on almost an identical number of carries—there shouldn't be any dropoff. PFF likes Hill quite a bit, though we have to keep in mind that their grading tends to go nuts about running backs, and his 2025 output was star-level. It's the OL that holds this group back.
Oregon does have a good center and we've seen Michigan get got to at least some extent by a few different teams with good centers and not a whole lot else. The weakness in the middle of Michigan's line isn't good for much other than some grinding 4-6 yard runs but teams have gotten those relatively often. This apparent weak spot may not be particularly exploitable with Oregon down to backup guards. This will be a slog unless Hill is able to make some magic on his own, which is a distinct possibility.
Raiola is a total nonfactor as a rusher, FWIW.
KEY MATCHUP: MICHIGAN vs TACKLING. The line yards here are going to be ugly for Oregon but they are Oregon and have a constant supply of dudes who you do not want to set free.
Pass Defense vs Oregon

Raiola: still aggressively mid? [Bryan Fuller]
Dante Moore was knocked for the year after that disgusting hit in the USC game, leaving former five star and Cornhusker Dylan Raiola as the starter—at least most of the time. Raiola's been about as up and down at Oregon as he was in Lincoln but has picked it up the last few weeks. Raiola got pulled from the UCLA game after throwing two picks en route to a 6/19, 2.2 YPA outing; third-stringer Brock Thomas was better statistically but loathed by PFF. Thomas got to start the next week, getting the hook after a 9/20, 2.7 outing.
From there Raiola has emerged as the top option. For another game and a half it looked like he was about to get yanked again but he has stepped it up the past two weeks, throwing for 336 yards at 10.8 yards a clip against Northwestern and 257 and 6.4 yards a pop against Ohio State. That latter doesn't seem different from a 6.0 YPA output against Illinois, but PFF graded that performance 20 points higher as Raiola played a defense that did not fire its coordinator after a handful of games. If you were so inclined you could suggest that Raiola is turning the corner.
Oregon's OL issues have not been as apparent in pass protection after the benching of erstwhile left tackle Ziyare Addison. Right tackle Fox Crader remains a big blinking DANGER sign for his own offense but nobody else is a capital-p Problem. The Ducks sit 24th in pass block grade and with Michigan's top two DEs probably limited they don't seem well equipped to take aim at Oregon's blinking sign. One caveat: IMO, teams that emphasize a bunch of short stuff can be overrated by PFF—I feel a similar pull when I chart 1/1 protection snaps—and Oregon's line drops pretty heavily on "true pass sets." (Everyone does but Oregon's drop is larger than most.) If Michigan is able to get the Ducks into passing situations the door will be more open than a top 25 PFF pass block grade might suggest.
Oregon's WR corps is the usual assortment of highly rated dudes but sophomore Dakorian Moore is approximately the only downfield threat. #1 WR Evan Stewart has an average depth of target around seven yards; tight end Jamari Johnson is another flex type who can shoot down the slot. This isn't exactly a hole for the Ducks but it is also not the flamethrowing unit it often is.
Michigan's defense has been very good this year and can probably hang with this pass offense, particularly without Moore. One thing I'm cautious about: man to man coverage on Moore. Jyaire Hill has crushed the big strong high point guys this year but has had some struggles with quicker athletes who can get him on a double move; Moore is emphatically that.
KEY MATCHUP: WELL THAT ONE. Hill's probably going to be in a bunch of man against a guy who is likely to be a first round pick down the road; if he can replicate the Becker performance against Indiana he's going to be one himself. Survey says: not quite.
SPECIAL TEAMS
Oregon has an iffy kicker situation and excellent punting. Gage Hurych is the kicker; he's 14/18 on largely short stuff and is 72nd in field goal efficiency. He also continues a burgeoning tradition of alarmingly named Oregon kickers after Atticus Sappington graduated.
Punter Bailey Ettridge has a 46 yard average and has given up –5 return yards this year. As in "negative five." On nine returns! That's hard to do. Oregon's nonstop fleet of incredible athletes who can be gunners probably helps out there.
Dakorien Moore and Evan Stewart have split punt return duties; neither has done much yet but could at any moment.
KEY MATCHUP: AHHH YOU PUT THE BALL THROUGH THE UPRIGHTS
INTANGIBLES

he's baaack
CHEAP THRILLS
Worry if…
This is not an attempt to be funny: what is left to worry about? I guess we could worry that Whittingham will return next year but I just don't see how that's possible. We could worry that people will leave for the portal but at this point I'm resigned to more or less the team entering the portal. The plane has crashed into the goddamned mountain.
Crystal Pepsi makes a return.
Cackle with glee if...
I suppose suddenly rushing for 300 yards against Oregon would be a situation in which I would cackle madly. I'm not sure "glee" would be an appropriate way to describe this, however. "Unsuccessful bid to retain my sanity" is much closer. Hmmm.
Cackle in an unsuccessful bid to retain your sanity if…
Michigan rushes for 300 yards because it was all Beck.

Fear/Paranoia Level: 0 (Baseline 5; –1 for We Have Migrated Past Fear, –1 for Paranoia Is For People Who Are Not The Hunted, –1 for What Would A Win Even Symbolize, –1 for When The Worst Has Come To Pass There Is Peace In The Rubble, –1 for Ah Fuck It)
Desperate Need To Win Level: 0 (Baseline 5; –1 for Season Over, –1 for Coaching Tenure Over, –1 for To Be Honest I Would Rather Not Eke Out A Spectacularly Unlikely Win, –1 for Checking Out Is Self-Care, –1 for I Can Sit At Home And Drink A Beer Instead Of Seeing This In Person)
Loss will cause me to... seize upon any message board tea leaf suggesting that Michigan is axing Whittingham posthaste.
Win will cause me to... 404 emotion not found.
The strictures and conventions of sportswriting compel me to predict:
Cumong man.
Finally, three opportunities for me to look stupid tomorrow:
A horse fights another horse!
It's horseageddon!
Oregon 32, Surviving Horse 6, Michigan 5

michigan.headline: OT: Gameday Cocktail If You're Also Sick Like Me: The Hot Toddy
michigan.body:
OT: Gameday Cocktail If You're Also Sick Like Me: The Hot Toddy

I seem to have come down with whatever the hell is going around.  I have a painful cough, muscle aches, and a general sense of dread (but that last one could be due to a lot of things).
In the past, when I've been sick on gamedays, I make Hot Toddies to drink.
Seems like a lot of families have their own variation on this, and here's mine:
Mug of hot, near boiling water
Plain black tea (bagged)
Squeeze of lemon
1 TBS of honey
1 1/2 oz of Southern Comfort
Mix the ingredients in the mug and let the tea steep for a moment before adding the SoCo; alcohol boils at a lower point than water (173F vs. 212F) so according to chemistry, the more you cool it down, the more potent the drink (no idea if the effect will be noticeable or not in this quantity)

michigan.headline: Michigan Mailbag: Was Kyle Whittingham forced to fire OC Jason Beck?
michigan.body:
The Michigan Wolverines are coming off a terrible loss to in-state rival Michigan State. Give credit to the Spartans and their coaching staff for putting up enough of a fight to beat Michigan. Despite injuries and only two wins before that game, they came to Ann Arbor and frustratingly beat the Wolverines.

Now, Michigan has a huge game at No. 16 Oregon this weekend. The Ducks fell off the map a bit after the injury to quarterback Dante Moore, but with a win at Ohio State last week, they look like a dominant team once again. They put up 41 points QB Dylan Raiola going for 25-of-40 for 257 yards and two touchdowns. That’s much improved after falling to Illinois just a few weeks ago.

We asked you to post some questions on The Feed earlier this week in anticipation of this week’s game.

On Michigan’s firing of OC Jason Beck

Head coach Kyle Whittingham said he made the decision after watching the tape on Sunday. It’s tough not to question whether that’s the truth, especially since he initially said he wasn’t going to make any decisions until after the season. For a man who doesn’t fully understand the Michigan-Michigan State rivalry, I’m inclined to believe there was pressure from somewhere, but that’s just speculation.

At the end of the day, Whittingham told everyone it was his decision. We’ll see if it’s actually going to make a difference.

On Michigan’s offensive struggles

Michigan’s offensive line is certainly struggling because of injuries to some of its players, but I really think the coaching staff and scheme didn’t help the team out that much. It also didn’t help that Tommy Carr has grown up a Michigan fan, understands this rivalry, and clearly had his nerves get the best of him. Passes sailed and he really struggled to avoid pressure, taking five sacks and “rushing” for -19 yards. It’s possible that firing Beck forces the Wolverines to ditch some things on offense that just haven’t been working.

I do think there are a few things that could be better against Oregon. First, it is possible to limit the turnovers. Michigan’s defense has also shown it can be better at forcing turnovers against teams that take chances throwing the ball. Michigan State called a pretty conservative offense last week, but that’s just not Oregon’s identity. The defense has a shot to really keep the offense in this game.

On interim OC Jim Harding

If you haven’t read it, Matt Hartwell did a nice job breaking down some of interim offensive coordinator Jim Harding’s history earlier this week. While Harding doesn’t have much experience calling plays, he has been part of some good offenses that leaned on the run game.

The Wolverines probably won’t look like a dynamic offense, but there’s a possibility they run more formations without using the rhino as much. Andrew Bailey really went in depth on some of those plays in his film study this week if you want to know more. It’s possible the Wolverines turn to a few blocking schemes and simplify the run game, which should help the running backs gain more yards per play.

Personally, I’m hoping the team rallies to play together. At times, it felt like every individual tried to play hero ball, and maybe now they’ll have a chance to rally. It’s clear some of the players weren’t bought into what Beck was trying to do. I imagine if it’s frustrating watching this team on the field, it’s just as frustrating to be on the field as a player.

If Harding wants to establish anything, my hope is he tries to let his guys outplay the other team rather than try to outsmart the Ducks. This offense hasn’t been good, but we know there are players who can make the plays. I have some optimism that Harding will allow his players to go out there and do what they know how to do — play football.

If you can’t tell, I’m trying to look at things as optimistically as I can. I feel like these players trusted this coaching staff, and the coaches have let them down this season. This weekend is an opportunity to change that.

As always, let’s keep the conversation going! Drop your thoughts in the comments below.
